it.title: IT support for New York small businesses.
it.summary: The printer has vanished again. Email will not send. The Wi-Fi reaches the front desk but stops at the back room. Tell us what changed; we’ll work through the cause and confirm what help is available.
it.description: Help with Mac, Windows, Microsoft 365, Wi-Fi and everyday tech. Clear explanations and account ownership. New York visits subject to confirmed availability.
it.body:
Tech support

Start with what stopped.

You do not need to diagnose the fault before you call. Tell us what happened, who it affects, and which part of the day has stopped.

  1. What changedThe message, outage, or behavior you noticed.
  2. Who feels itThe people, rooms, devices, or customers affected.
  3. What cannot waitWhat needs to work first so you can carry on.

A small map beats a big guess

Find the break before changing anything.

We check what still works and where the trouble begins. For Wi-Fi, that might mean testing the connection near the router, then in the rooms where you actually use it. That helps us tell an internet-provider issue from a problem inside the space.

What should stay private?

Do not send passwords, recovery codes, payment data, or private customer records in a support request. Share the symptom first and agree on a safe access method.

Read the Wi-Fi guide +

The first useful record

Know what we fixed.

You should be able to explain the fix without learning a new vocabulary. We leave a plain account of what changed, who controls it, and what to check next.

Symptom
What staff or customers saw.
Scope
Which work, devices, rooms, or accounts were affected.
Change
What we changed and which account controls it.
Next check
What to check if the problem returns.

Everyday systems

Get help with the tools you use.

Wi-Fi, printers, and payment devices

Map where the connection fails and what still works before moving equipment or changing settings. A guest network, a card reader, and a staff laptop may need different checks. If a card reader has been taking payments offline, do not sign out, reinstall, or reset it until those payments have uploaded, or they can be lost.

Outlook, Microsoft 365, and business email

Look at the message path, mailbox rules, and account owner. In Microsoft 365, check shared-mailbox access, licenses, and who can administer the account. Preserve the mail and files the business needs before a staff handover.

Check business email +
Mac, iPhone, iPad, and Windows setup

List the tasks that must work on day one. Test email, files, printing, calls, and the connection where you will use the device. Check the work account, the sign-in app on the phone, and the recovery route. Keep the old device until you can sign in on the new one, and sign it out of its Apple Account or work account before it is erased or passed on.

Plan a device handover +

Choosing IT help in New York

Test any provider on one small job.

Good IT help names the real problem, writes down what changed, and leaves the business less dependent on memory, including ours. Ask these four questions of anyone you are considering.

How do you handle passwords?
The answer should never be by text or email. Access is agreed in a safe way, and the accounts stay in the business name.
Will I get a note after each fix?
Yes: the symptom, what changed, which account controls it, and what to check next time.
What happens if I stop paying you?
You keep every login: the domain, email, Google Business Profile, hosting and devices.
Do I need a monthly contract?
Not with us. Scoped, written work comes first, and regular check-ins are there if you want them.

When a visit makes sense

Plan around the work that must stay on.

Tell us your New York neighborhood and what needs attention. Many problems start with a remote diagnosis by phone or text. When hands are needed, we confirm visit availability, access and the work involved before you make plans; a visit is booked only when we confirm it with you.

Your accounts stay yours. If a provider or equipment vendor needs to act, we explain who to contact and what they need to know.

Accounts
stay yours.

consulting.title: Know what to fix first.
consulting.summary: A new tool looks useful. The bill says otherwise. Bring the quote, the monthly charges, or the task that keeps getting stuck. We help you decide what is worth changing.
consulting.description: Technology consulting for small businesses. Review software costs, compare vendor quotes, and decide what to fix before paying for a change.
consulting.body:
A practical second opinion

Put the real work on the table.

Bring the vendor quote, the subscription bill or the process everyone works around. We look at what customers experience and what your team has to do to keep things moving.

We explain the choices, the likely disruption and the questions to settle before you spend. Working tools can stay.

One path at a time

Follow the work from hello to follow-up.

Take one booking, order, or inquiry and follow it through the business. Where does someone wait, copy a detail, or ask the same question again?

  1. They askWhere does the first question arrive?
  2. You answerCan the customer tell what to do next?
  3. The work movesWho gets the request, and what do they do with it?
  4. You can see itWhere is the record when someone needs it?

A decision with a reason

Keep, connect, or change.

A change has to be worth its cost and the time your team will spend learning it. We weigh both before recommending one.

Keep it

A working tool with a clear owner may be worth leaving alone. That conclusion can save a business from an expensive project with no real job.

Connect it

Your booking tool may already share the details another system needs. Check what each tool allows, who controls the accounts, and how staff will use the connection.

Change it

If the same problem keeps coming back, agree on one change and how to test it. A new system comes after we understand the work.

Clarity in public

Give people a path they can understand.

ClearHelp is a public Little Fight website built around people’s situations and locations. It shows the same practical idea: let a person begin with the question they actually have.

See the ClearHelp case study +

After the conversation

A decision should outlive the meeting.

You leave with the recommendation and its reasons: what to change, what it depends on, and what can wait. Put it in front of your team or a vendor and everyone can discuss the same decision.

Problem
The customer or work issue behind the decision.
Evidence
The tool, bill, quote, or path you reviewed.
Decision
What changes now and what stays put.
Owner
Who can approve, maintain, and revisit it.

software.title: Give the busywork a better home.
software.summary: The same order goes into two systems. An approval gets buried in a text. We look at the task, then decide whether your current tools can handle it or a small custom tool would help.
software.description: Custom small-business software for bookings, approvals and repeated work. Explore real Little Fight products, a focused first build and clear ownership.
software.body:
Custom software

Find the task you keep doing twice.

Show us one real example, from the first request to the finished job. We look for the point where someone has to copy a detail, chase an answer, or check which version is right.

  1. It startsA request, booking, sale, or question arrives.
  2. It gets copiedSomeone repeats it in a second place.
  3. It needs a homeThe next person needs a reliable record.

Real product work

One record can carry a whole night.

VenueCircuit was built around a specific repeated task: closing a venue night while keeping venue and promoter money distinct. It keeps the night’s figures together so people can check how each share was worked out.

See VenueCircuit +

Small enough to use

Build the first useful part.

Start with one task people can use in a normal workday. Try it with the team. The missed detail or unusual request will tell us more than a long list of features.

Follow the task from start to finish

Who starts the task? Who checks it? What happens when something is missing? Agree on those details before asking software to handle them.

Test it in the actual workday

Try an ordinary task and an awkward one. The useful detail often appears where a real customer, staff member, or record does not fit the first assumption.

Decide from evidence

Once people have used the first change, the next decision can come from what happened in the work instead of a long feature list.

A system your business can carry

Keep the keys to the work.

Before building, we agree on the scope, ownership and care plan. You know where your code and data live, who controls the accounts, and which outside services have their own costs.

Files
The project files go to the place named in your written plan.
Data
You know where records are stored and how to get them back.
Accounts
Your business controls who can sign in and make changes.
Notes
The next person has instructions for running and maintaining it.

Little Fight Labs

Try a working idea.

Explore Growth Street, one of our interactive studies. Try the experience, picture what a useful interaction could do for your business, and return here when you’re ready.

brand.title: Problems? Solved.
brand.summary: The shop is open. The office is busy. The website, Wi-Fi, and back-office work should keep up. Tell us where the day gets stuck.
brand.description: Custom websites, New York tech support, consulting and software for independent businesses. Explore real Little Fight NYC work and talk to a person.
brand.body:
Little Fight NYC

There is a business behind the screen.

A customer is trying to book. Someone at the desk is looking for a file. You are trying to finish the work. We build websites and sort out the technology around those ordinary moments.

Four useful paths

Start with the shape of the problem.

WebsitesHelp customers choose you.+Tech supportKeep the work moving.+ConsultingKnow what to fix first.+Custom softwareGive the busywork a better home.+

A clear answer earns the next step

Answer the question people actually have.

Can a customer find your hours? Can your team find the right file? Can someone see who needs to approve an order? We build around those everyday questions so people can get on with what they came to do.

  1. A real questionWhat is broken? What should we choose? Can this be simpler?
  2. A plain answerSpecific enough to help a person decide.
  3. A human next stepCall, text, email, or write when the work needs a person.

Built for a real business

The detail should fit the work.

After Hours Agenda is an independent clothing brand. Its website brings the story and lookbook together, with a place to follow future releases. New orders are paused while the next collection is developed.

See After Hours Agenda +

A clear beginning

Bring the thing that is in the way.

Send the website, error message, or quote you want us to look at. A few lines in your own words are enough. The first look is free; you approve the scope and price before paid work starts.

Little Fight
NYC

faq.a: Begin with the work that is blocked, expensive, confusing, or repeated. A current website, an error message, a vendor quote, or a short description of the task gives us something real to review.

faq.q: Can you help if I do not know the technical name for the problem?
faq.a: Yes. Describe what changed, who is affected, and what work cannot move. The first conversation can identify the useful category and the next safe check.

faq.q: Do you work outside New York?
faq.a: Website work can be scoped remotely. New York on-site support availability is confirmed after the issue, location, access rules, equipment, and schedule are understood.
